exposure: gestational age (34-35 weeks vs. >=36 weeks) in infants with moderate to severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE)
outcome: brain injury patterns detected on MRI
time to achieve full enteral feeding
blood gas parameters (pH, base deficit, lactate)
cohort: The cohort consisted of 20 late preterm infants (34-35 weeks GA) and a matched cohort of 80 term infants (>=36 weeks GA), all diagnosed with moderate to severe Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) and treated with therapeutic hypothermia.
finding: Late preterm infants (34-35 weeks GA) treated with therapeutic hypothermia for HIE experienced lower birth weights, higher rates of caesarean delivery, increased need for inotropes, longer time to full enteral feeding, longer hospital stays, and distinct brain injury patterns (e.g., more thalamic/cerebellar abnormalities) compared to term infants (>=36 weeks GA) with HIE treated similarly, despite comparable overall brain injury rates on MRI.
mod_finding: Late preterm infants (34-35 weeks GA) had a significantly higher rate of caesarean delivery compared to term infants (>=36 weeks GA).
birth_weight: Lower in infants with GA of 34-35 weeks compared to infants with GA of >=36 weeks.
